Empirical Research Plan: Credit‐Supply Shocks, Small-Business Lending, and Real Outcomes

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Instrumental-variables (IV) difference-in-differences using a shift–share (“Bartik”) instrument.

• Idea County-year variation in small-business credit supply is predicted by the pre-crisis portfolio composition of the banks that already served that county.  
• First stage For each county c and year t we construct:
 PredictedCreditShockc,t = Σb (RealEstateExposureb,2006 × PreCtyShareb,c,2006) × PostCrisis t  

 – RealEstateExposureb,2006 = share of bank b’s assets in 1-4 family mortgages + construction & land development loans in 2006.  
 – PreCtyShareb,c,2006 = bank b’s share of total CRA small-business loans in county c in 2006.  
 – PostCrisis t = 1 for 2008–2010, 0 otherwise.

This instrument isolates the part of the within-county credit contraction driven by bank-specific balance-sheet distress, not by contemporaneous local demand conditions.  
• Second stage Estimate the causal impact of (instrumented) county-level small-business lending on employment and output measures from CBP.

Why appropriate?  
(i) Supply shock: cross-bank heterogeneity in real-estate exposure is predetermined.  
(ii) Local demand fixed effects: county (or county×industry) FE absorb time-invariant differences; year FE absorb common shocks.  
(iii) Bartik design is standard in credit-supply literature (e.g., Greenstone–Mas (2013); Ciminelli et al. 2021).

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
• Δlog(SBLend)c,t = change in log CRA small-business loan dollars per worker (or per establishment) in county c, year t.

Instrument (treatment intensity)  
• PredictedCreditShockc,t described above.

Control group / counterfactual  
• Counties whose pre-crisis bank mix implies little or no predicted credit shock (bottom quartile of PredictedCreditShock distribution).  
• In the regression framework all counties are retained; identification comes from continuous variation in instrument.

Treatment timing  
• Shock window 2008–2010 (main); pre-period 2004–2007 for parallel-trend tests; 1996–2003 used to estimate county trends.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A1 Relevance Banks with higher pre-crisis real-estate exposure cut SBL significantly more during 2008–2010. (Testable; F-stat > 10 expected.)

A2 Excludability (Exogeneity) Conditional on county FE, year FE, county trends, and pre-crisis housing-cycle controls, the pre-crisis bank-mix-based instrument affects employment/output only through contemporaneous small-business credit supply.

Plausibility: Bank portfolios set largely at headquarters level and before the shock; controlling for local housing bust further reduces violations.

A3 Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-county spillovers) Predicted credit shock in county c does not directly affect firms in county c’. Plausible because small-business lending tends to be local; we cluster SEs at the commuting-zone level as an extra safeguard.

A4 Parallel trends in outcome conditional on controls Absent the credit shock, employment trends in high- and low-exposed counties would have evolved similarly after conditioning on trends and controls. We will test this using event-study coefficients 2004–2010.

A5 No endogenous migration of banks across counties in response to impending crisis. We lock bank-county weights at 2006 to avoid this issue.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
T1 Correlation with local housing bust (demand).  
 Mitigation: control for pre-crisis and contemporaneous house-price growth, foreclosure rates, construction employment share; include county×industry pre-trends; restrict sample to non-construction industries in robustness checks.

T2 Measurement error in CRA loan data (e.g., reporting thresholds).  
 Mitigation: winsorize extreme growth rates; validate with FDIC Call Report totals; robustness excluding very small counties; instrumentation alleviates attenuation bias.

T3 Bank branch network confounds (e.g., banks headquartered in boom regions).  
 Mitigation: compute instrument using only out-of-county branches or only multi-county banks; add HQ-state×year FE; leave-one-out version of instrument (drop bank b when predicting county c in which it is HQed).

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages -----------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # fast high-dim FE + IV
library(lmtest); library(sandwich)

# 1. Load Data ----------------------------------------------------------------
cra   <- fread("CRA_smallbiz_1996_2010.csv")      # bank-county-year
call  <- fread("CallReports_1996_2010.csv")       # bank-quarter
cbp   <- fread("CBP_county_1996_2010.csv")        # county-year
house <- fread("CoreLogic_HPI_county_1998_2010.csv") # optional control

# 2. Construct Bank-Level Exposure -------------------------------------------
# Annualise Call Reports
call[, year := year(quarter)]
exp_vars <- c("1_4fam_loans", "const_land_loans", "total_assets")
call_year <- call[, lapply(.SD, mean, na.rm=TRUE), 
                  by = .(cert, year), .SDcols = exp_vars]
call_year[, RE_exposure := (1_4fam_loans + const_land_loans)/total_assets]

# Freeze exposure at 2006
exp2006 <- call_year[year==2006, .(cert, RE_exposure_06 = RE_exposure)]

# 3. BankCounty Pre Crisis Loan Shares ---------------------------------------
# CRA small business loans; keep 2006 as base year
cra06 <- cra[year==2006, .(loan_amt = sum(sbl_amt, na.rm=TRUE)),
             by = .(cert, county_fips)]

# Compute within-county shares
cra06[, county_total := sum(loan_amt), by = county_fips]
cra06[, share06 := loan_amt/county_total]

# Merge exposure
cra06 <- merge(cra06, exp2006, by="cert", all.x=TRUE)

# 4. Build Shift–Share Instrument --------------------------------------------
# Post-crisis indicator
years <- 1996:2010
post  <- data.table(year = years, Post = as.integer(year >= 2008))

# Cartesian join to create county-year panel
cty_year <- CJ(county_fips = unique(cra06$county_fips), year = years)

# Merge post and house-price controls
cty_year <- merge(cty_year, post, by="year")

# Compute predicted credit shock: Σ_b exposure_b * share_b,c * Post_t
pred <- merge(cty_year, cra06, by="county_fips", allow.cartesian=TRUE)
pred[, PredShock := sum(RE_exposure_06 * share06 * Post), 
     by = .(county_fips, year)]
pred <- unique(pred[, .(county_fips, year, PredShock)])

# 5. Construct Outcomes -------------------------------------------------------
# Small biz lending
cra_cty <- cra[, .(SBL = sum(sbl_amt, na.rm=TRUE)), 
               by=.(county_fips, year)]
cra_cty[, logSBL := log1p(SBL)]  # log(1+SBL)

# Employment from CBP
emp <- cbp[, .(Emp = sum(emp, na.rm=TRUE)), by=.(county_fips, year)]
emp[, logEmp := log(Emp)]

# Merge all
panel <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y, all=TRUE, by=c("county_fips","year")),
                list(pred, cra_cty, emp, house))

# Controls
panel[, dHPI := c(NA, diff(log(hpi))), by = county_fips]

# 6. First Stage --------------------------------------------------------------
fs <- feols(logSBL ~ PredShock | county_fips + year, data=panel, cluster="county_fips")
summary(fs)

# 7. Second Stage (IV) --------------------------------------------------------
iv_main <- feols(logEmp ~ 1 | county_fips + year | (logSBL ~ PredShock), 
                 data=panel, cluster="county_fips")
summary(iv_main)

# 8. Robustness: leave-one-out instrument ------------------------------------
# Drop within-county HQed banks
cra06_nonHQ <- cra06[bank_hq_county != county_fips]
# (Repeat steps 4–7 with new instrument)

# 9. Event-Study / Pre-trend Check -------------------------------------------
es <- feols(logEmp ~ sunab(Post, year, ref.p=2007) | county_fips, 
            data=panel, cluster="county_fips")
iplot(es)  # requires fixest 0.11+
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory and past evidence suggest a positive elasticity of employment with respect to small-business credit. Prior: A 10 percent IV-predicted decline in SBL leads to a 1–2 percent fall in county small-firm employment over 2008–2010, with larger effects in credit-dependent industries (manufacturing, retail).

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = satisfied, 0 = questionable)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Instrument relevance (F-stat > 10) …….................................................... 1  
2. Exogeneity / exclusion (after controls) ….......................................... 0.7  
3. No differential pre-trends (event study) …...................................... 0.8  
4. No spillovers / SUTVA …........................................................... 0.8  
5. Data quality / measurement error …............................................ 0.7  

Average ≈ 0.8 → overall methodology reasonably credible, but exogeneity remains the main caveat.
